The word remains ordinary eating. Zen bends it by putting the unexceptional act into public answers and tests, without making every meal a metaphor.

SearchAliases: Zen do not get it wrong
Senses.Explanation: An imperative: do not (莫) understand or take it (會) wrongly (錯). Its distinct Chan deployment is as warnings that named speakers attach directly to a saying or answer in public discourse. Asked the intention of the coming from the West, Anguo Hongtao answers 'it is so, but do not get it wrong.' An extended address says not to infer 'not round and not sudden' from the preceding words and not to present borrowed, similar, or calculated phrases as one's own understanding, repeating 'do not get it wrong.' Elsewhere Bao’en Huiming warns an assembly not to say that speech, silence, movement, and stillness are all buddha-affairs. The formula can also follow an unexplained seasonal statement — 'yesterday snow, today it melts' — leaving the warning itself as the only explicit appraisal. These contexts establish the public-interview function without supplying an interpretation of what the preceding words secretly mean.
